CS163 · Caltech · Reconstruction study

Recovering ABRs from simulated noisy EEG

Evaluated configurations: 4 / 4 · Two priors, two training seeds

Question and design

Can a trained diffusion prior recover a reference ABR from a known pulse train and simulated noisy recording? The primary outcome is mean per-observation waveform reconstruction RMSE, not v-prediction error. For each reconstruction: RMSE = sqrt(mean((estimated ABR − reference ABR)²)) × 0.1 µV per model unit.

New CNN models are trained independently on analytic waveforms and EARNDB template augmentations, with two training seeds. Each uses 60,000 available training waveforms, batch size 32, AdamW, EMA, and 1,000 optimizer updates. Checkpoints at 200, 400, 800 and 1,000 are assessed with guidance 0, 0.3, 1 and 3 on validation cases. The checkpoint/guidance pair with minimum validation RMSE is frozen before test evaluation. Three sampling seeds assess stochastic sensitivity. A six-value ridge grid is tuned on the same validation observations.

The architecture is held fixed: a 7,745-parameter temporal CNN with 16 channels and six residual convolution blocks at dilations 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32. Training predicts v using mean squared error under a 200-step cosine diffusion schedule. AdamW uses learning rate 2×10⁻⁴ and weight decay 10⁻⁴, gradients are clipped at norm 1, and EMA uses rate 0.005. Examples are sampled with replacement: 1,000 updates at batch size 32 means 32,000 waveform presentations, not 1,000 epochs.

Analytic ABRs vary peak timing, width and amplitude, include a trough and optional early component, and are filtered at 80–1,500 Hz; 10% are null waveforms. EARNDB ABR averages are restricted to SPL≥70 dB and ABR channels identified by nV headers. Digital waveforms have DC removed using the epoch tail, are resampled from 48 to 10 kHz, and are normalized to synthetic 0.04 µV RMS. The periodic epoch tail supplies the negative-time portion of the window; it is not measured pre-onset EEG. Template augmentation uses log-normal gain (log SD 0.2) and shifts from −0.3 to +0.3 ms with zero padding. No test subject contributes to these training templates.

EARNDB subjects N1–N5 train the prior, N6 provides validation references, and N7–N8 provide test references. Four reference targets per domain are used in validation and eight per domain in testing (four references each from N7 and N8); each has white/colored noise at synthetic 0.05/0.20 µV standard deviation, giving 32 validation observations and 64 test observations. Analytic targets use independent split seeds. All methods share paired recordings. Observation duration is 0.2 seconds. RMSE is computed over 256 waveform samples, then averaged over observations and sampling seeds. Repeated noisy observations and seeds are not independent subjects.

Forward model: EEG = stimulus matrix × reference ABR + noise. Diffusion sampling uses 200 reverse steps and an EEG-residual gradient. The clean reference is excluded from that gradient. Trace RMSE measures the estimated clean ABR at each step; final test RMSE measures the returned reconstruction.

CoreWeave Forge: training, validation reconstruction and sampling traces

Results

Observed test RMSE ranges from 0.01930 to 0.02097 µV. Tuned ridge reaches 0.02461 µV (relative penalty 1, selected on validation). The lowest observed test value belongs to analytic_cnn_29; this is descriptive and was not used to select or tune a model.

Key findings

  • Analytic prior: mean held-out reconstruction RMSE 0.01944 µV, 21.0% lower than the tuned ridge baseline in this pilot.
  • EARNDB template prior: mean held-out reconstruction RMSE 0.02091 µV, 15.0% lower than the tuned ridge baseline in this pilot.
  • On ANALYTIC reference targets: analytic prior 0.01396 µV; template prior 0.02064 µV. The domain-specific comparison is more informative than the pooled score alone.
  • On EARNDB reference targets: analytic prior 0.02492 µV; template prior 0.02118 µV. The domain-specific comparison is more informative than the pooled score alone.
  • 4 of 4 configurations selected the strongest tested guidance (3.0). For these configurations, the guidance optimum is not bracketed by this grid.

1 · Training convergence

Each line is an independent training seed. This objective measures v prediction; reconstruction is evaluated separately below.

2 · Reconstruction-based checkpoint selection

At each checkpoint, guidance is chosen by validation RMSE. The minimum over checkpoints determines the selected model. No test score enters this selection.

3 · Guidance strength

Validation reconstruction error at the selected checkpoint. A minimum at the edge of the tested grid means the optimum has not been bracketed.

4 · Held-out reconstruction and noise robustness

Models use validation-selected checkpoints and guidance. Curves average the training and sampling seeds; shading is the range of training-seed means, not a confidence interval. Ridge regularization is selected on validation cases.

5 · Inside the reconstruction loop

Reference ABRs are used only to record diagnostic error; they never enter sampling gradients. The clean estimate can fluctuate during stochastic sampling. These curves are not a guarantee of monotonic convergence or calibrated uncertainty.

6 · Reconstructed waveform examples

Examples are the first test waveform in each domain under high colored noise, selected by fixed index rather than quality. Colored lines are the mean across training and sampling seeds; shading spans all individual reconstructions and is not a calibrated credible interval. Quantitative RMSE tables average individual reconstruction errors rather than scoring this ensemble mean.

7 · Baseline regularization

The ridge coefficient is selected by the minimum on this validation grid. The test set is evaluated once using that selected coefficient.

Interpretation and limits

This is a small reconstruction-focused pilot. Only one EARNDB participant supplies validation targets and two supply a balanced set of test targets; the number of waveforms does not establish population-level certainty. Template references are measured averages with residual noise and are normalized to synthetic 0.04 µV RMS. Their physical calibration is unresolved. Results measure recovery of those references in simulated EEG, not performance on real continuous EEG. No probability intervals or significance claims are made.

The early training budget tests checkpoint selection, not maximum attainable performance. Guidance-grid boundary minima should motivate a separately specified validation sweep. A lower denoising loss need not imply lower reconstruction RMSE, and a lower EEG residual need not imply a more accurate ABR. The high-noise waveform examples illustrate that lower average RMSE can coexist with attenuated response peaks. RMSE alone does not establish faithful peak amplitude or timing; the raw test tables also provide waveform correlation and a descriptive 3–10 ms peak-timing error, which is not a validated clinical wave-V annotation. Future improvements should be selected on validation data; repeated test inspection can bias subsequent comparisons.

Reproduction and provenance

EARNDB v1.0.0: PhysioNet dataset, ODC Attribution license. Silva & Epstein (2010), Estimating loudness growth from tone-burst evoked responses, JASA 127:3629–3642, doi:10.1121/1.3397457. Downloaded record hashes are preserved in the data manifest.
